phy_ocrb.2.0.summary: Static electricity happens when two insulating materials are rubbed together and **electrons are transferred** from one surface to the other: the object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the one that loses them is left positively charged by the same amount. **Like charges repel and unlike charges attract**, and every charged object is surrounded by an **electric field**, a region where another charge feels a non-contact force. The idea of a field explains attraction of neutral objects by induction, the shocks you get from car doors and carpets, and sparks such as lightning when the field is strong enough to ionise the air.

core.h: Atoms, charge and why only electrons move
core.p: All matter is made of atoms containing positive protons in a tiny nucleus and negative electrons around it. A neutral object has equal numbers of protons and electrons so the charges cancel. Protons are locked inside nuclei, but outer electrons are held much more weakly, so **only electrons are transferred** when objects become charged.
bullets: Proton charge = +1 unit, electron charge = −1 unit (same size, opposite sign).
Neutral means equal numbers of + and − charges, not 'no charges'.
**Gaining electrons** makes an object negative.
**Losing electrons** makes an object positive; positive charges never move onto it.
Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**; one electron carries about 1.6 × 10^-19 C.

callouts.p: Never write that 'positive charges moved onto the cloth'. A positively charged object has **lost electrons**.

core.p: When two different insulators are rubbed together, the friction brings the surfaces into very close contact and **electrons are transferred** from one material to the other. Which way they go depends on the materials: some hold electrons more strongly than others. Because electrons are only moved, not created or destroyed, the two objects end up with **equal and opposite charges**.
bullets: Polythene rubbed with a wool cloth: electrons move from cloth to polythene, so **polythene becomes negative** and the cloth positive.
Acetate (perspex) rubbed with a cloth: electrons move from acetate to cloth, so **acetate becomes positive** and the cloth negative.
Charge is **conserved**: total charge before = total charge after (zero).
Insulators keep the charge where it was rubbed because electrons cannot flow through them.
A metal held in the hand will not stay charged: electrons flow through the metal and your body to or from earth.

callouts.p: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, **electrons are transferred** from one to the other; the material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the material that loses electrons becomes positively charged.

core.p: Charged objects exert forces on each other without touching. **Like charges repel and unlike charges attract**. The force is a non-contact force and it gets **weaker as the distance between the charges increases**, and stronger for larger charges.
bullets: Two negatively charged polythene rods push apart (repel).
A negative polythene rod and a positive acetate rod pull together (attract).
Forces come in pairs: each object feels an equal and opposite force (Newton's third law).
A suspended charged rod that swings away from another rod proves they have the **same** type of charge.
**Repulsion is the only sure test** for a charge, because attraction also happens between a charged and a neutral object.

callouts.p: Like charges repel; unlike (opposite) charges attract. The closer the charges, the bigger the force.

core.p: A charged object creates an **electric field** around itself. The field is the region in which another charged object experiences a **non-contact force**. Fields are how forces act at a distance: the first charge sets up the field, and the second charge feels a force because it is in that field.
bullets: The direction of the field is the direction of the force on a **small positive** test charge.
Field lines point **away from positive** charges and **towards negative** charges.
Field lines never cross.
**Closer lines = stronger field**; the field is strongest close to the charged object.
The field gets weaker with distance, which is why the force decreases as charges move apart.
A negative charge in a field feels a force opposite to the direction of the field lines.

callouts.p: A region around a charged object in which another charged object experiences a non-contact force.

fig.cap: Electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere. Field lines are radial (like spokes of a wheel) and evenly spaced around the sphere, pointing outwards from a positive sphere and inwards towards a negative sphere. The lines spread out with distance, showing that the field gets weaker further away.

core.h: Drawing field patterns: how to score the marks
core.p: OCR expects you to draw the field around an **isolated charged sphere**. Examiners check three things: the lines are radial, they have arrows in the correct direction, and they start or end on the surface of the sphere.
bullets: Draw at least 8 straight lines that would meet at the centre if extended.
Lines must **touch the surface** at right angles to it.
Put an arrow on **every** line: outward for +, inward for −.
Space them evenly; do not let them cross or curve.
You may be asked to explain the spacing: lines further apart = weaker field.

callouts.p: Forgetting arrows is the most common way to lose the mark on a field diagram.

core.p: Whether charge stays put depends on the material. In **conductors** such as metals, some electrons are free to move through the material, so charge spreads out or flows away to earth. In **insulators** such as plastic, rubber, glass and dry air, electrons are not free to move, so charge stays where it was placed.
bullets: Static charge builds up on **insulators**.
A conductor can only be charged if it is **insulated** from earth (for example on a plastic stand).
**Earthing**: connecting a charged conductor to the ground with a conductor lets electrons flow to or from earth until it is neutral.
Damp air or a damp surface lets charge leak away, which is why static effects are weaker on humid days.

core.p: A charged object can attract a **neutral** object. The field of the charged object pushes or pulls electrons within the neutral object so that the near side gains the **opposite charge** and the far side gains the same charge. This separation is called **induced charge**. The opposite charges are closer, so the attraction is bigger than the repulsion, giving a **net attractive force**.
bullets: **Charged balloon on a wall**: a negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface near the balloon positive; the balloon is attracted and sticks.
**Charged comb picking up paper**: a comb charged by combing hair induces opposite charge on the near side of small paper bits; attraction outweighs their weight, so they jump up.
A charged rod bends a thin stream of water towards it in the same way.
The neutral object stays **neutral overall**: charge is only rearranged, not added.
Force is larger at smaller distance, which is why near-side attraction beats far-side repulsion.

callouts.p: Do not say the wall 'is positive'. The wall is neutral overall; only its surface near the balloon has an **induced** positive charge.

fig.cap: A negatively charged balloon near a neutral wall. Its field repels electrons in the wall surface away from it, so the near surface is left with an induced positive charge. Opposite charges are closer than like charges, so attraction wins and the balloon sticks to the wall.

core.p: You can become charged by friction, for example walking on a nylon carpet, sliding out of a car seat or taking off a jumper. Your body is insulated from the ground by your shoes, so the charge builds up. When you touch a conductor connected to earth, such as a metal door handle, tap or car door, **electrons suddenly flow** between you and earth, and you feel a small shock.
bullets: Walking on carpet: electrons transfer between shoes and carpet, charging you.
Getting out of a car: friction between clothes and the seat charges you; touching the metal door discharges you.
The shock is a brief current: charge flowing to make you neutral again.
Often a tiny **spark** jumps the last millimetre before you touch.
Anti-static wrist straps, conductive flooring or damp air prevent charge building up.

core.p: If enough charge builds up, the **electric field** between a charged object and a nearby earthed object becomes very strong. A strong field can pull electrons off air molecules, **ionising the air**. Ionised air conducts, so charge suddenly flows through it as a **spark**. Lightning is a giant spark.
bullets: In a thundercloud, collisions between ice particles and water droplets transfer electrons, so the **bottom of the cloud becomes negative**.
The negative cloud base induces a positive charge on the ground below.
The field between cloud and ground grows until the air is ionised.
Electrons rush to earth along the ionised path: a lightning strike.
Sparks are dangerous near flammable vapours (fuel tankers, aircraft refuelling), so vehicles are **earthed** to let charge flow away safely.
Sparks happen more easily at sharp points because the field is strongest there.

callouts.p: Large charge → strong electric field → air molecules ionised → air conducts → charge flows suddenly as a spark.

fig.cap: Lightning. Charge separation in the cloud leaves its base negative, which induces positive charge on the ground. The electric field between them becomes strong enough to ionise the air, which then conducts, and a huge spark carries charge to earth.

core.p: Static charge can be a nuisance or dangerous, but understanding it lets us prevent problems. The key idea every time is to give the charge a **safe conducting path to earth** so it never builds up.
bullets: Fuel tankers and aircraft are **earthed** with a conducting cable before fuel flows, so a spark cannot ignite vapour.
Dust is attracted to charged TV screens and plastic surfaces by induction.
Clothes cling after a tumble dryer because they become charged by friction.
Electronics workers wear earthing straps so sparks do not damage chips.
Lightning conductors give lightning a safe path to earth down the outside of a tall building.

core.p: Six-mark questions reward a logical chain of cause and effect. For any static effect, explain where the electrons go, what charge that leaves, and what force or flow results.
bullets: Step 1: name the two materials and the **friction** between them.
Step 2: state which way **electrons** are transferred.
Step 3: state the resulting charges (equal and opposite).
Step 4: describe the **electric field** and the force (like repel / unlike attract, or induction).
Step 5: if a shock or spark happens, explain **electron flow to or from earth**.

callouts.p: Answers that say only 'charge moved' usually miss the mark. Say **electrons** are transferred.

analogy.p: Imagine two people each holding a bag with equal numbers of red (positive) and blue (negative) marbles. Rubbing is like one person grabbing a handful of blue marbles from the other: now one bag has extra blue (negative) and the other is short of blue, so its red marbles are not cancelled (positive). Only blue marbles can be grabbed, just as only electrons move. The analogy breaks down because marbles do not push or pull on each other from a distance, whereas charges exert forces through their electric fields, and real charge is spread over a surface rather than stored inside a container.

terms.d: A tiny negatively charged particle found outside the nucleus of an atom; the only charged particle that moves when objects are charged by friction.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus; its charge is equal in size to an electron's but opposite in sign.
Electric charge that builds up and stays on the surface of an insulator.
Rubbing two insulators together so that electrons are transferred from one surface to the other.
Having more electrons than protons, because electrons have been gained.
Having fewer electrons than protons, because electrons have been lost.
A region around a charged object in which another charged object experiences a non-contact force.
A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive charge; closer lines mean a stronger field.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as the electrostatic force.
A material in which electrons are free to move, so charge can flow through it.
A material in which electrons are not free to move, so charge stays where it is placed.
A separation of charge in a neutral object caused by a nearby charged object's electric field.
Connecting an object to the ground with a conductor so that charge can flow away and it becomes neutral.
A sudden flow of charge through air that has been ionised by a strong electric field.
Removing electrons from atoms or molecules so they become charged ions; ionised air conducts.
Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, so the total charge stays the same.

mistakes.w: Positive charges moved from the rod to the cloth.
mistakes.r: Only **electrons** move; the rod became positive because it **lost electrons** to the cloth.

mistakes.w: Rubbing creates charge.
mistakes.r: Rubbing **transfers** electrons; charge is conserved and the two objects gain equal and opposite charges.

mistakes.w: The balloon sticks because the wall is positively charged.
mistakes.r: The wall is neutral overall; the balloon **induces** a positive charge on the near surface by repelling electrons, so attraction is greater than repulsion.

mistakes.w: Field lines around a positive sphere point inwards.
mistakes.r: Field lines point in the direction of the force on a positive charge, so they point **away from positive** and towards negative.

mistakes.w: Attraction proves an object is charged.
mistakes.r: Neutral objects are also attracted by induction; only **repulsion** proves an object is charged with the same sign.

mistakes.w: The shock is caused by friction from touching the door.
mistakes.r: The shock is caused by **electrons flowing** between the charged person and the earthed metal (discharge).

mistakes.w: A spark happens because electrons jump through empty space.
mistakes.r: The strong electric field **ionises the air**, making it conduct so charge can flow through it.

mistakes.w: Metals can't be charged.
mistakes.r: A metal can be charged if it is **insulated from earth**; otherwise electrons flow through it to or from earth.

exam.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a duster and becomes negatively charged. Explain how the rod becomes negatively charged.
model: Friction/rubbing transfers electrons.
Electrons move from the duster to the rod, so the rod gains electrons.
exam.tip: Say electrons are gained by the rod; never mention positive charges moving.

exam.q: State the charge left on the duster in the question above.
model: Positive (equal in size to the rod's negative charge).
exam.tip: Equal and opposite is worth stating.

exam.q: Two negatively charged rods are brought close together. Describe what happens.
model: They repel / push apart because like charges repel.
exam.tip: Give the rule as your reason.

exam.q: Draw the electric field pattern around an isolated positively charged sphere.
model: Radial lines touching the surface, evenly spaced.
Arrows on lines pointing outwards (away from the sphere).
exam.tip: Arrows on every line, pointing away from positive.

exam.q: Define an electric field.
model: A region in which a charged object experiences a (non-contact) force.
exam.tip: Include 'charged' and 'force'.

exam.q: Explain why the force between two charged spheres decreases as they are moved apart.
model: The electric field gets weaker with distance from a charge.
So a charge further away experiences a smaller force.
exam.tip: Link force to field strength.

exam.q: A negatively charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Explain why.
model: Balloon's negative charge/field repels electrons in the wall surface.
Near surface of the wall gains an induced positive charge.
Unlike charges attract, so the balloon is attracted to the wall.
Attraction greater than repulsion because opposite charges are closer.
exam.tip: The closer-charges point is what gets the fourth mark.

exam.q: A comb is pulled through dry hair and then picks up small pieces of paper. Explain this.
model: Friction transfers electrons between hair and comb so the comb becomes charged.
Comb's field causes charge separation in the paper (induction).
Opposite charge is induced on the side of the paper nearest the comb.
Attractive force is bigger than the paper's weight, so the paper is lifted.
exam.tip: Work through the step chain: transfer, charge, induction, force.

exam.q: A person walks across a nylon carpet and then gets a shock touching a metal door handle. Explain why.
model: Friction between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the person.
The person is insulated from earth (shoes), so charge builds up.
Touching the earthed metal lets electrons flow suddenly to/from earth: a current felt as a shock.
exam.tip: Mention insulation from earth to explain why the charge builds up.

exam.q: Explain how lightning occurs and why fuel tankers are earthed before refuelling. Use ideas about charge and electric fields.
model: Collisions/friction between particles in the cloud transfer electrons.
The base of the cloud becomes negatively charged.
This induces a positive charge on the ground.
A very strong electric field forms between cloud and ground.
The field ionises the air, which then conducts and electrons flow suddenly to earth as a spark (lightning).
Fuel flowing through pipes charges the tanker by friction; earthing lets charge flow away safely so no spark can ignite fuel vapour.
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover both parts with a clear chain of reasoning.

worked.q: An acetate rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. Explain what has happened to the electrons and the charge on the cloth.
steps: Rubbing (friction) transfers electrons between the surfaces.
The rod is positive, so it must have lost electrons.
Those electrons moved onto the cloth.
Charge is conserved, so the cloth gains a negative charge equal in size to the rod's positive charge.
worked.ans: Electrons moved from the acetate rod to the cloth, so the rod is positive and the cloth has an equal negative charge.

worked.q: A rod carries a charge of −3.2 × 10^-9 C after rubbing. How many extra electrons does it have? (charge on an electron = 1.6 × 10^-19 C)
steps: Number of electrons = total charge ÷ charge on one electron.

worked.q: A student holds a charged rod near a suspended rod and it swings towards it. Can she conclude the suspended rod is charged?
steps: Attraction also happens between a charged and a neutral object, by induction.
So attraction does not prove the suspended rod is charged.
She should test for repulsion with a rod of known charge.
worked.ans: No: attraction could be induction of a neutral rod; only repulsion proves it is charged (with the same sign).

phy_ocrb.2.1.summary: An electric current is a **flow of charge**; in metal wires the charges that move are **free electrons**, which are already present in the wire before the circuit is switched on. The size of the current is the **rate of flow of charge**, so **charge = current × time (Q = I t)**, with charge in coulombs, current in amperes and time in seconds. A current only flows when there is a **closed loop** and a source of potential difference, and in a single loop the current is the same everywhere because charge is not used up. You must also be able to recognise, draw and use the standard **circuit symbols**.

core.p: An electric current is a **flow of electric charge**. In a metal wire the moving charges are **free electrons** (delocalised electrons) that can drift between the fixed positive metal ions. The battery does not supply the electrons; they are **already in every part of the circuit**. The battery provides a push (a potential difference) that makes all of them drift round the loop at the same time.
bullets: In metals: current = flow of **free electrons**.
In solutions (electrolytes): current = flow of **ions**.
Charges are **not used up** in a component; the same number return to the battery as leave it.
What a component uses is **energy**, carried by the charges, not the charges themselves.
Because charges are everywhere in the loop, a lamp lights almost instantly when the switch closes.

callouts.p: The **rate of flow of charge** around a circuit.

core.h: Conditions for a current to flow
core.p: Two things are needed for a steady current: a **closed circuit** (a complete conducting loop with no gaps) and a **source of potential difference** such as a cell, battery or power supply. If any gap appears, for example an open switch or a broken filament, the charges cannot flow anywhere in the loop and the current stops everywhere at once.
bullets: Open switch → gap → **no current** anywhere in that loop.
A cell on its own with no loop gives no current.
Wires are good conductors so they let charge flow easily.
Insulators in the loop (plastic, air gap) stop the current.

callouts.p: A current needs a **closed loop** and a **potential difference**.

core.h: Charge, current and time: Q = I t
core.p: Current tells you how much charge passes a point every second. One **ampere** is a flow of one **coulomb per second**. So if you know the current and how long it flows, you can find the total charge that has passed.
bullets: **charge (C) = current (A) × time (s)**
Q = I × t, so I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I.
Charge is measured in **coulombs, C**.
Current is measured in **amperes (amps), A**; small currents in milliamps (1 mA = 0.001 A).
Time must be in **seconds**: convert minutes (× 60) and hours (× 3600) first.

callouts.p: A current of 1 ampere is a flow of 1 coulomb of charge per second.
Most lost marks come from leaving time in minutes or current in mA. Convert first.

core.p: Scientists decided the direction of current before electrons were discovered. **Conventional current** is shown flowing from the **positive terminal to the negative terminal** around the outside of the circuit. We now know electrons are negative, so they actually drift the **opposite way**, from negative to positive. Both describe the same current.
bullets: Arrows on circuit diagrams show **conventional current**: + to −.
Electrons flow − to + (they are attracted to the positive terminal).
The long thin line of a cell symbol is the **positive** terminal.
Diodes and other one-way components are drawn with the arrow showing conventional current.

core.p: In a **series circuit (single closed loop)** the current has the **same value at every point**. Charge is conserved: it cannot pile up anywhere or be destroyed, so the rate at which charge passes one point must equal the rate at any other point.
bullets: Ammeters placed anywhere in a single loop give the **same reading**.
Current is **not used up** by lamps or resistors.
Adding more components in series makes the current smaller, but still the same everywhere.
This is why one broken lamp in a series string makes all the lamps go out.

callouts.p: Current is the same at any point in a single closed loop.

core.p: Where a circuit branches, the current splits. Because charge is conserved, the **total current into a junction equals the total current out of it**. The branch with less resistance takes more current.
bullets: I in = sum of I out.
Branch currents add up to the current from the battery.
This is a consequence of conservation of charge.
Detailed parallel-circuit rules are covered with series and parallel circuits.

bullets: Break the circuit and insert the ammeter into the loop.
Never connect an ammeter in parallel across a component.
Choose a range that fits (A or mA) for precise readings.
Check for a **zero error** before taking readings.
Digital ammeters give a reading directly; analogue ones need you to read the scale at eye level.

bullets: Use a ruler; draw the circuit as a rectangle.
Join wires at junctions with a **dot**.
Put each meter in the correct place (A in series, V across the component).
Do not draw a voltmeter in the main loop.
Label components if asked (e.g. 'R1').

core.h: Why current is a rate: thinking about charge flow
core.p: A bigger current does not mean faster electrons alone; it means **more coulombs pass each second**. In a metal the free electrons actually drift slowly (fractions of a millimetre per second), but there are enormous numbers of them, so even a small drift gives a measurable current.
bullets: Each electron carries a tiny charge of about 1.6 × 10^-19 C.
1 C is the charge of about 6 × 10^18 electrons.
So a 1 A current means about 6 × 10^18 electrons pass every second.
Doubling the current doubles the charge passing per second.

analogy.t: Water in a closed central-heating loop
analogy.p: Think of a sealed loop of pipes completely full of water, with a pump. The water (charge) is already in every pipe. Switching the pump on makes all the water move at once, and the flow rate in litres per second (current in coulombs per second) is the same at every point in a single pipe loop. At a T-junction the flow splits but the total is conserved. The pump does not create water, just as a battery does not create electrons. The analogy breaks down because water can leak out of a broken pipe, whereas charges cannot leave a broken wire; in a circuit a gap simply stops the flow everywhere. Also, the 'water' in a wire is negatively charged electrons moving opposite to the conventional current.

terms.d: The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
A property of particles such as electrons and protons; measured in coulombs (C).
The unit of charge; the charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s.
The unit of current; 1 A is a flow of 1 coulomb per second.
Electrons in a metal that are not bound to one atom and can drift through the metal to form a current.
A complete conducting loop with no gaps, needed for a current to flow.
Current direction drawn from the positive terminal to the negative terminal round a circuit.
The actual drift of electrons, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
A circuit with only one path (a single loop); the current is the same at every point.
A point where a circuit branches; current in equals total current out.
Charge is not created or used up, so current is not used up in a circuit.
A meter that measures current; connected in series and has a very low resistance.
A meter that measures potential difference; connected in parallel across a component.
A single source of potential difference; a battery is two or more cells.
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large.
A component that lets current flow in one direction only.

mistakes.r: Current is the **same everywhere in a single loop**; charge is conserved. Energy is transferred, not charge.

exam.q: State the unit of charge.

exam.tip: Do not confuse C (coulomb) with current.

phy_ocrb.2.2.summary: **Resistance** is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current: for a given potential difference, the bigger the resistance, the smaller the current. Resistance is defined by **R = V ÷ I** and is used as **potential difference = current × resistance (V = I R)**, with resistance measured in **ohms (Ω)**. Resistance arises because free electrons **collide with the vibrating ions** of the metal lattice. In PAG7 you measure the resistance of a wire at different lengths with an ammeter and a voltmeter and find that **resistance is directly proportional to length** at constant temperature.

core.p: Every component opposes the flow of charge to some extent. **Resistance** tells you how much potential difference is needed to drive each ampere of current through a component. A component with a high resistance lets only a small current through for a given p.d.; a low-resistance component lets a large current through.
bullets: Resistance is measured in **ohms (Ω)**.
1 Ω means 1 V is needed to push 1 A through the component.
For a fixed p.d., **bigger resistance → smaller current**.
For a fixed resistance, **bigger p.d. → bigger current**.
Connecting wires have very low resistance; resistors, lamps and heaters have higher resistance.

callouts.p: Resistance = potential difference ÷ current (R = V / I). It measures how much a component opposes the current.

core.p: The defining relationship links the three quantities. You need to recall it and rearrange it confidently in any form.
bullets: **potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω)**
V = I × R
I = V ÷ R
R = V ÷ I
Always convert mA to A (÷ 1000) and kΩ to Ω (× 1000) before substituting.
Give the unit with your answer: V, A or Ω.

callouts.p: V = I R. It is on the equation sheet as a recall equation, so you must know it from memory.

core.p: A metal is a lattice of **positive ions** with **free electrons** drifting between them. As the electrons move, they **collide with the ions**, transferring energy to them. This makes the ions vibrate more, so the metal **heats up**. These collisions are what oppose the current, and they are the reason for resistance.
bullets: More collisions per second → larger resistance.
Collisions transfer energy from the electrons to the lattice as **thermal energy** (heating).
When the metal is hotter, the ions **vibrate more**, so electrons collide more often, so **resistance increases with temperature**.
This heating effect is used in kettles and toasters but wastes energy in cables.

core.h: Factors affecting the resistance of a wire
core.p: The resistance of a metal wire depends on its **length**, its **cross-sectional area** (thickness), the **material** and its **temperature**. Each of these changes how many collisions an electron makes on its way through.
bullets: **Length**: longer wire → more ions to collide with → resistance increases; R is directly proportional to L.
**Thickness**: thicker wire → more paths for electrons side by side → **lower** resistance.
**Material**: nichrome and constantan have much higher resistance than copper of the same size.
**Temperature**: hotter wire → ions vibrate more → higher resistance.
Copper is used for connecting wires because its resistance is low.

core.p: For a metal wire or fixed resistor **at constant temperature**, the current is **directly proportional** to the potential difference. Doubling V doubles I, so V ÷ I (the resistance) stays constant. Such components are called ohmic conductors.
bullets: A graph of I against V is a **straight line through the origin**.
The resistance is the same at every point on the line.
This only holds if the **temperature stays constant**.
If the wire heats up, its resistance rises and the line curves (as for a filament lamp).

callouts.p: Always add 'at constant temperature' when stating that current is proportional to p.d. for a wire.

core.h: PAG7: investigating resistance of a wire — apparatus
core.p: In this practical you find how the resistance of a wire depends on its **length**. The wire (often constantan or nichrome) is taped along a **metre ruler**. One crocodile clip stays at the zero end and the other is moved to set the length. An **ammeter in series** measures the current and a **voltmeter in parallel** across the chosen length measures the p.d.
bullets: Low-voltage d.c. power supply (or cell).
Ammeter connected **in series**.
Voltmeter connected **in parallel** across the test length only.
Test wire fixed to a metre ruler with two crocodile clips.
A switch, so current flows only while readings are taken.

core.p: The method needs to change only one variable (length) and keep everything else the same, so any change in resistance is caused by the length.
bullets: Set the clips 20 cm apart (measure from the inside edges with the ruler).
Close the switch, read the **current** and **p.d.** quickly, then open the switch.
Calculate **R = V ÷ I**.
Repeat for lengths of 30, 40, 50 ... 100 cm.
Repeat each length two or three times and calculate a **mean** resistance.
Plot a graph of **resistance (y-axis) against length (x-axis)** and draw a line of best fit.

callouts.p: Independent: length. Dependent: resistance (from V and I). Control: material, thickness (diameter), temperature.

core.p: The graph of resistance against length is a **straight line through the origin**, so resistance is **directly proportional** to length. Doubling the length doubles the resistance. The gradient of the line gives the resistance per metre of that wire.
bullets: Straight line → linear relationship; through origin → directly proportional.
Gradient = change in R ÷ change in L (units Ω/m).
A thicker wire of the same material gives a line with a **smaller gradient**.
If the line does not go through the origin, suspect a **systematic error** such as contact resistance at the clips or a zero error on the ruler.

core.p: The biggest problem is that current **heats the wire**, raising its resistance and spoiling the results. Good technique keeps the temperature constant and makes each reading as accurate as possible.
bullets: Use a **low p.d./small current** to reduce heating.
**Switch off between readings** so the wire can cool.
Avoid very short lengths: the current would be large and the wire hot.
Make sure the wire is **straight and not kinked**, so the length measured is the true length.
Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax.
Contact resistance at the clips can add a small constant extra resistance.
Safety: the wire can get **hot enough to burn**; do not touch it while current flows.

callouts.p: Students forget to say how they keep the temperature constant. 'Switch off between readings' and 'use a small current' are the marks.

core.h: Using V = I R in circuits
core.p: You can use V = I R for a single component or for the whole circuit, as long as V, I and R all refer to the **same** part. For a component, use the p.d. across that component and the current through it.
bullets: Find R from meter readings: R = voltmeter reading ÷ ammeter reading.
A variable resistor changes R and so changes I for the same supply p.d.
If R increases while V stays the same, I decreases in proportion: doubling R halves I.
Checking units first prevents factor-of-1000 errors.

core.h: Interpreting graphs of V and I
core.p: In exams you might be given an I–V or V–I graph and asked to find the resistance. Always calculate R = V ÷ I using a **point on the line**; for a straight line through the origin this equals the gradient of a V against I graph or 1 ÷ gradient of an I against V graph.
bullets: Read V and I from the same point; check the axis units.
Steeper I–V line → **lower** resistance.
Shallower I–V line → **higher** resistance.
A curve means resistance is changing; calculate R at a specific point.

callouts.p: On an I (y) against V (x) graph, the gradient is 1/R, not R.

analogy.p: Picture pupils (electrons) being pushed down a corridor by a teacher (the battery's p.d.). Pillars along the corridor (metal ions) get in the way, and pupils bump into them. A longer corridor has more pillars, so more bumping and slower overall flow: higher resistance. A wider corridor lets more pupils pass side by side: lower resistance. If the pillars started shaking about (a hotter wire), there would be even more collisions. A harder push from the teacher (bigger p.d.) gets more pupils through per second (bigger current). The analogy breaks down because real electrons are all pushed at the same moment throughout the wire, and each collision transfers energy that heats the lattice, which pupils bumping pillars would not do.

terms.d: The ratio of potential difference across a component to the current through it, R = V / I; a measure of opposition to current.
The unit of resistance; 1 Ω = 1 volt per ampere.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts with a voltmeter in parallel.
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter in series.
Potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω).
A conductor in which current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature, so its resistance is constant.
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Electrons in a metal that can move between the ions and carry the current.
The fixed positive metal ions that free electrons collide with, causing resistance.
The area of the end face of a wire; a larger area (thicker wire) gives a lower resistance.
The variable you deliberately change; in PAG7, the length of the wire.
The variable you measure; in PAG7, the resistance found from V and I.
A variable kept the same so it cannot affect the result, such as wire material, thickness and temperature.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount, such as a zero error or contact resistance.
Unpredictable scatter in readings; reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed to control the current in a circuit.

mistakes.w: R = I ÷ V or R = V × I.
mistakes.r: **R = V ÷ I**; V = I R.

mistakes.w: Uses 250 mA as 250 A in V = I R.
mistakes.r: Convert to **0.25 A** before substituting.

mistakes.w: Resistance is how much current is used up.
mistakes.r: Resistance is the **opposition to current**: the p.d. needed per ampere (V/I). Current is not used up.

mistakes.w: A longer wire has less resistance because electrons have more room.
mistakes.r: A longer wire has **more** resistance: more ions to collide with, R ∝ L.

mistakes.w: Thicker wire has more resistance because there is more metal.
mistakes.r: A thicker wire has **less** resistance: more electrons can flow side by side.

mistakes.w: Current is proportional to voltage for a wire.
mistakes.r: Only **at constant temperature**; if it heats up its resistance increases.

mistakes.w: Puts the voltmeter in series with the wire.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter goes **in parallel** across the length being tested; the ammeter goes in series.

mistakes.w: Says the graph shows 'R increases with L' and stops.
mistakes.r: State that R is **directly proportional** to L because the graph is a straight line **through the origin**.

mistakes.w: Keeps the wire switched on throughout to save time.
mistakes.r: **Switch off between readings** and use a low current to keep the temperature constant.

exam.q: State the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
model: potential difference = current × resistance (V = I R).
exam.tip: Words or symbols both score.

exam.q: A resistor has a p.d. of 6.0 V across it and a current of 0.30 A. Calculate its resistance.
exam.tip: Include the unit Ω.

exam.q: A 2.2 kΩ resistor carries a current of 5.0 mA. Calculate the p.d. across it.
exam.tip: Convert both prefixes.

exam.q: A 12 V supply is connected to a 48 Ω heater. Calculate the current.
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons, why a metal wire has resistance.
model: Free electrons collide with the (positive) ions in the metal lattice.
This opposes their flow / transfers energy to the ions.
exam.tip: 'Collide with ions' is the key phrase.

exam.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal wire increases when it gets hotter.
model: The ions vibrate more at higher temperature.
So electrons collide with them more often.
exam.tip: Link vibration to more collisions.

exam.q: Describe how the resistance of a wire depends on its length and its thickness.
model: Resistance is (directly) proportional to length / longer means higher resistance.
Thicker wire has lower resistance.
exam.tip: Answer both parts.

exam.q: In PAG7 a student finds the line of R against L does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason.
model: Contact resistance at the clips / zero error on the ruler or meter (systematic error).
exam.tip: Name a systematic error.

exam.q: Suggest two ways the student can keep the temperature of the wire constant during PAG7.
model: Use a low p.d./small current.
Switch off between readings to let the wire cool.
exam.tip: Two separate, practical actions.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length. Include the equipment, the measurements and how you would use them.
model: Wire taped to a metre ruler; crocodile clips set the length.
Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the test length, with a power supply.
Measure V and I for a range of lengths (e.g. 0.1 m to 1.0 m in 0.1 m steps).
Calculate R = V ÷ I for each length; repeat and take means.
Keep temperature constant: low current, switch off between readings; same wire material and thickness.
Plot R against L; a straight line through the origin shows R is directly proportional to L.
exam.tip: A full answer covers set-up, measurements, control and analysis.

worked.q: In PAG7, at a length of 0.60 m the voltmeter reads 1.24 V and the ammeter reads 0.40 A. Find the resistance and predict the resistance of 0.90 m of the same wire.
steps: R is directly proportional to L, so R per metre = 3.1 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 5.2 Ω/m.
worked.ans: 3.1 Ω at 0.60 m; about 4.7 Ω at 0.90 m.

The p.d. across a 15 Ω resistor is increased from 3.0 V to 6.0 V at constant temperature. Find the current before and after.
steps: Doubling V doubles I because R is constant (ohmic).

phy_ocrb.2.3.summary: An **I–V characteristic** is a graph of current against potential difference for a component, and its shape tells you how the component's **resistance** behaves. A fixed resistor (or wire) at constant temperature is **ohmic**: a straight line through the origin, so its resistance is constant. A **filament lamp** curves because its resistance increases as it heats up, a **diode** only lets current flow in one direction, and the resistance of an **LDR falls as light intensity increases** while the resistance of a **thermistor falls as temperature increases**. In PAG6 you measure these characteristics with an ammeter, a voltmeter and a way of varying the p.d., reversing the supply to get negative values.

core.p: An I–V characteristic is a graph of **current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis)** for one component. At any point, the resistance is **R = V ÷ I**. If the line is straight through the origin, V ÷ I is the same everywhere, so resistance is constant. If the graph curves, the resistance is changing as the current changes.
bullets: Positive V and I: current one way; negative values: supply reversed.
**Steeper** line = more current per volt = **lower** resistance.
**Flatter** line = **higher** resistance.
Always calculate R from V ÷ I at a point, not from the gradient of a curve.
The shape is a 'fingerprint' that identifies the component.

callouts.p: Most OCR graphs plot I on the y-axis. Some plot V on the y-axis, which flips the meaning of 'steep'. Check before answering.

core.p: To find an I–V characteristic you need to measure the current through the component and the p.d. across it for a range of p.d. values. The **ammeter is connected in series** with the component and the **voltmeter in parallel** across it. A **variable resistor** (or a variable d.c. power supply) changes the p.d.
bullets: d.c. power supply or battery.
Variable resistor in series to change the current and p.d.
Ammeter in series with the component.
Voltmeter in parallel across the component only.
Component under test: fixed resistor, filament lamp, diode (with a protective resistor), LDR or thermistor.
A switch so the current is only on when readings are taken.

core.p: Take readings over a wide range of p.d. in **both directions** so the whole characteristic is plotted, including negative values.
bullets: Set the variable resistor to give the smallest p.d.; record V and I.
Change the variable resistor in steps to increase V; record V and I each time (at least 8 readings).
**Reverse the connections** to the supply (or to the component) and repeat to get negative values.
Repeat readings and calculate means to reduce random error.
Plot I (y-axis) against V (x-axis) with the origin in the middle and draw a smooth curve or line of best fit.
Take more readings where the graph changes shape quickly (e.g. around 0.6 V for a diode).

callouts.p: For the fixed resistor, switch off between readings so it stays at constant temperature. For the lamp, the heating is the effect you are studying, so let each reading settle.

core.p: For a fixed resistor or a metal wire **at constant temperature**, current is **directly proportional** to p.d. The graph is a **straight line through the origin**, and the same in both directions. Because V ÷ I is constant, the resistance is constant.
bullets: Straight line through origin → I ∝ V.
Same shape for negative V: it conducts equally well both ways.
Steeper line → smaller resistance.
Resistance = V ÷ I at any point (equals 1 ÷ gradient).
Only true if the temperature does not change.

callouts.p: Current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature, so resistance stays constant.

fig.cap: I–V characteristics. Left: a fixed resistor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin. Centre: a filament lamp gives an S-shaped curve that gets flatter at higher p.d. because its resistance increases as it heats up. Right: a diode lets almost no current flow in reverse, then conducts once the forward p.d. is above about 0.6 V.

core.p: A filament lamp is a thin metal wire that gets very hot. At small p.d. the line starts fairly straight, but as the current increases the filament heats up, its **resistance increases**, and the graph **curves and gets flatter**. The same happens in reverse, giving a symmetrical S-shape.
bullets: Bigger current → more collisions between electrons and metal ions → filament gets hotter.
Hotter metal → ions **vibrate more** → electrons collide more often → **resistance increases**.
So each extra volt gives a smaller increase in current: the curve flattens.
Symmetrical: reversing the p.d. gives the same shape in the negative quadrant.
A lamp is **non-ohmic** because its temperature changes.

callouts.p: current increases → temperature increases → ions vibrate more → more collisions → resistance increases → graph gets less steep.

core.p: A diode lets current flow in **one direction only** (the forward direction, shown by the triangle in its symbol). In the reverse direction it has a **very high resistance** so the current is almost zero. In the forward direction the current is tiny until the p.d. reaches about **0.6 V** (for a silicon diode), after which the resistance falls rapidly and the current rises steeply.
bullets: Reverse direction: very high resistance, current ≈ 0.
Forward, below about 0.6 V: very little current.
Forward, above about 0.6 V: low resistance, current increases rapidly.
Used to protect circuits from a supply connected the wrong way and to convert a.c. to d.c. (rectification).
Always put a **protective resistor** in series with a diode in PAG6 so the current cannot get too large.
An **LED** (light-emitting diode) behaves the same way and emits light when current flows forwards.

callouts.p: A component that allows current to flow in one direction only; it has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

core.p: An LDR is made of a semiconductor. Its **resistance decreases as light intensity increases**. In bright light more charge carriers are released in the material, so current flows more easily. In the dark its resistance is very high.
bullets: Bright light → **low** resistance → bigger current.
Dark → **high** resistance → small current.
At a **constant light level** its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin.
Brighter light makes that line **steeper**.
Uses: automatic street lights, night lights, light meters, burglar alarms.

fig.cap: Resistance graphs for sensors. Left: the resistance of an LDR falls as light intensity increases. Right: the resistance of a (negative temperature coefficient) thermistor falls as temperature increases. Both fall steeply at first and then level off.

core.p: A thermistor is also a semiconductor. The common type (NTC) has a **resistance that decreases as its temperature increases**. Heating it releases more charge carriers, so it conducts better when hot. This is the **opposite** of a metal wire, whose resistance rises with temperature.
bullets: Hot → **low** resistance; cold → **high** resistance.
At a fixed temperature its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin; hotter → steeper.
If a large current heats it, its resistance falls and the I–V graph curves **upwards** (gets steeper).
Uses: thermostats, electronic thermometers, fire alarms, engine temperature sensors.
LDRs and thermistors are used in sensing circuits (covered with potential dividers).

callouts.p: Filament lamp: hotter → resistance **up**. Thermistor: hotter → resistance **down**.

core.h: LDR I–V lines at different light levels
core.p: If the light level is held constant, an LDR behaves like a fixed resistor and gives a straight-line I–V graph. Changing the light level changes the gradient, which is how a question may test you.
bullets: Two lines through the origin: the steeper line is the brighter condition.
Use R = V ÷ I at any point to compare resistances.
The same idea works for a thermistor at two temperatures: the steeper line is the hotter one.

fig.cap: I–V lines for an LDR at two constant light levels. In bright light the resistance is low, so the line is steeper; in dim light the resistance is higher, so the line is less steep.

core.p: Questions often ask you to read a point from a graph and calculate resistance, or to compare resistances at two points to show the resistance is changing.
bullets: Pick a point; read V and I carefully including units (mA!).
R = V ÷ I.
For a lamp, compare R at low and high p.d.: R increases.
For a diode, R in reverse is extremely large because I ≈ 0.
Quote your answer with Ω and sensible significant figures.

core.p: Good technique makes the characteristic reliable and safe to measure.
bullets: Check meters for **zero errors** before starting.
Use a range of at least 8–10 readings, in both directions.
Use a **protective resistor** with the diode so the current cannot exceed its rating.
Lamp filaments and resistors get **hot**: do not touch them.
Keep the resistor cool (switch off between readings); keep light level or temperature constant for the LDR or thermistor.
Repeat readings to identify anomalies and reduce random error.

analogy.p: A fixed resistor is like a corridor of fixed width: push twice as hard and twice as many people get through each second. A filament lamp is a corridor that gets more crowded and chaotic the more people you push through, so each extra push helps less and less (resistance rises). A diode is a turnstile: easy one way once you push past a small 'click' (about 0.6 V), but locked the other way. An LDR is a corridor whose doors open wider when the lights come on, and a thermistor opens wider when the heating comes on. The analogy breaks down because electrons are pushed by a p.d. throughout the whole circuit at once, and the real reasons (ion vibrations, release of charge carriers in semiconductors) are about particles, not doors.

terms.d: A graph of current against potential difference for a component.
R = V ÷ I; the p.d. needed per unit current, measured in ohms.
A conductor in which current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature.
A component whose resistance changes as the current or conditions change, so its I–V graph is not a straight line.
A lamp with a thin metal filament whose resistance increases as it gets hotter.
A component that allows current in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse.
Connecting a diode so that current can flow through it in its allowed direction.
Connecting a diode the opposite way so it has very high resistance and almost no current flows.
The forward p.d. (about 0.6 V for a silicon diode) above which a diode conducts well.
Light-emitting diode: a diode that emits light when current flows in the forward direction.
Light-dependent resistor: its resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
A temperature-dependent resistor; for an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases.
A material such as silicon whose number of charge carriers, and so its resistance, depends on conditions like light and temperature.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed to vary the current and p.d. in a circuit.
A resistor placed in series with a component such as a diode to limit the current.
Change in current ÷ change in p.d.; for a straight line through the origin it equals 1 ÷ R.

mistakes.w: The lamp's resistance decreases as it gets brighter.
mistakes.r: The filament's resistance **increases** as it gets hotter, because ions vibrate more and electrons collide more often.

mistakes.w: The resistance of a thermistor increases with temperature.
mistakes.r: For a thermistor (NTC), resistance **decreases** as temperature increases.

mistakes.w: An LDR's resistance increases in bright light.
mistakes.r: An LDR's resistance **decreases** as light intensity increases.

mistakes.w: A diode has zero resistance in the forward direction.
mistakes.r: It has a **low** resistance above about 0.6 V; below that it conducts very little.

mistakes.w: A steeper I–V line means more resistance.
mistakes.r: With I on the y-axis, a steeper line means **less** resistance (more current per volt).

mistakes.w: Resistance of the lamp = gradient of the curve.
mistakes.r: Calculate **R = V ÷ I** at a point on the curve.

mistakes.w: Only takes positive readings in PAG6.
mistakes.r: **Reverse the connections** to get negative p.d. and current values.

mistakes.w: A resistor is always ohmic.
mistakes.r: Only **at constant temperature**; heating changes its resistance.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter connected across the variable resistor or whole circuit.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter must be **in parallel across the component** being tested.

exam.q: Sketch the I–V characteristic of a fixed resistor at constant temperature.
model: Straight line through the origin (into both positive and negative quadrants).
exam.tip: Draw it through the origin and into both quadrants.

exam.q: State how the resistance of a thermistor changes as its temperature increases.
model: It decreases.
exam.tip: One word answer; do not confuse with a lamp.

exam.q: State how the resistance of an LDR changes when the light intensity increases. Suggest one use of an LDR.
model: Resistance decreases.
Automatic street light / night light / light sensor.
exam.tip: Give a specific use.

exam.q: Describe the I–V characteristic of a diode.
model: Current is (almost) zero in the reverse direction / very high resistance.
Little current forward until about 0.6 V.
Above this, current increases rapidly (low resistance).
exam.tip: Cover reverse, threshold and forward behaviour.

exam.q: A filament lamp has a p.d. of 2.0 V and current 0.20 A; at 6.0 V the current is 0.40 A. Use calculations to show how its resistance changes.
model: Resistance increases as p.d./current increases.
exam.tip: Two calculations then a comparison.

exam.q: Explain why the I–V graph of a filament lamp is curved.
model: As current increases the filament gets hotter.
The metal ions vibrate more.
Electrons collide with the ions more often, so resistance increases.
So current increases less for each extra volt and the graph gets less steep.
exam.tip: Full chain from current to graph shape.

exam.q: Draw a circuit diagram to show how you could measure the I–V characteristic of a filament lamp.
model: Lamp in series with supply and variable resistor/variable supply.
Ammeter in series with the lamp.
Voltmeter in parallel across the lamp.
exam.tip: Use correct symbols.

exam.q: Why should a protective resistor be connected in series with a diode during PAG6?
model: To limit the current so the diode (or meters) is not damaged when it conducts.
exam.tip: Above 0.6 V the current rises very fast.

exam.q: Two I–V lines for the same LDR are plotted; line A is steeper than line B. Which was in brighter light? Explain.
model: Line A.
Steeper line means lower resistance, and LDR resistance is lower in brighter light.
exam.tip: Link gradient → resistance → light.

exam.q: Describe how to obtain the full I–V characteristic for a filament lamp, and describe and explain the shape of the graph you would expect.
model: Circuit: lamp with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel; variable resistor or variable supply.
Vary the p.d. in steps and record V and I; repeat for accuracy.
Reverse the supply connections to obtain negative values.
Plot I against V.
Graph: S-shaped curve through origin, symmetrical, getting less steep at higher p.d.
Because the filament heats up, ions vibrate more, more collisions, so resistance increases.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs method, shape and explanation.

worked.q: From a diode's I–V graph: at 0.70 V the current is 25 mA, and at −2.0 V the current is 0.001 mA. Calculate the resistance in each case and comment.
steps: The reverse resistance is enormously larger, so the diode effectively only conducts one way.
worked.ans: About 28 Ω forward and about 2 MΩ in reverse: a diode conducts in one direction only.

worked.q: A thermistor has a p.d. of 6.0 V across it. At 20 °C the current is 2.0 mA; at 60 °C the current is 12 mA. Find its resistance at each temperature.
steps: The resistance falls as temperature rises, as expected for a thermistor.

worked.q: A student's I–V graph for a component is a straight line through the origin that passes through (4.0 V, 0.16 A). Identify a likely component and find its resistance.
steps: Straight line through origin → ohmic → fixed resistor at constant temperature.
